B1.why: It states the timeline doesn't justify choosing an individual to blame and moves the focus to the upgrade, alert routing, escalation and recovery controls. The decision questions ask 'what made that choice reasonable then?', and it warns against hindsight 'Why didn't you just…?' framing. It stays practical and doesn't dismiss the manager: it acknowledges the VP's Friday deadline and gives usable language for the VP.

B2.why: It rejects the inattention account using the facts available: the runbook-prescribed silence, the 14 prior deploy flaps and the competing urgent export request. It asks what would have distinguished this page from earlier flaps 'using what you could see at 16:31', and what checks the runbook required before silencing. That reconstructs what he saw and faced instead of just asserting he was rational.

B3.why: It declines to close the review on more alerts. Its reason is that the pool-saturation warning already fired at 16:22 and a latency page reached the on-call, so the gap is why those signals didn't lead to intervention, including whether the pool warning was routed appropriately. It doesn't explicitly name alert noise as a cost of adding more alerts, and 'add a pool alert if it closes a demonstrated detection gap' is a soft concession. Still, the core reason, that the alert existed but didn't reach someone who acted, is given.
